newsitem.title: USA: U.S. jobless rate dips to 5.2 percent in March.
newsitem.headline: U.S. jobless rate dips to 5.2 percent in March.

text.p: The unemployment rate edged down to 5.2 percent last month from 5.3 percent in February as job growth slowed slightly, but remained respectable and fairly broad-based, the government said on Friday.
The Labor Department said 175,000 non-farm jobs were added to payrolls in March, fewer than the 293,000 that were created in February and slightly less than had been expected.
Economists surveyed by Reuters had forecast an unemployment rate of 5.2 percent, and an increase of 196,000 in non-farm payrolls.

The report, the government's first look at the health of the economy in March, had been anxiously awaited in financial markets, where traders had been nervously watching for signs of whether the labour market would tighten to the point of triggering wage-driven inflation.
Last week Federal Reserve policy-makers lifted short-term interest rates by a quarter percentage point due to concern that strong consumer spending could set off inflationary wage and price rises.

Federal Reserve Board Vice Chairman Alice Rivlin told Reuters Financial Television on Thursday that the economy had was still strong in the first quarter, after growing at a vigorous 3.8 percent pace in the last three months of 1996, and that labour markets are quite tight.
While the 175,000 jobs created last month lagged the monthly average payroll growth of 225,000 of the past 12 months, workers' earnings have been edging upward, the department said.

In March average hourly wages rose by 5 cents to $12.15, after edging up a revised 5 cents in February, instead of the previously reported 3 cents, the department said. Over the past 12 months, wages rose 4 percent, matching their highest growth rate since the 12 months ended June 1990, it said.
The March payrolls increase occurred almost entirely in private service industries, which added 187,000 jobs, the department said.
Job growth included 58,000 in business services, including 25,000 temporary help jobs, as well as 22,000 in health services and 43,000 in retailing, it said.
The manufacturing sector added 16,000 jobs in March, bringing the growth since last September to 74,000, it said.
Factory overtime hours rose by 12 mintues to 4.9 hours per week, while the factory work week also rose by 12 minutes to 42.1 hours.

The volatile construction industry, which added 108,000 jobs in February, lost 27,000 jobs last month, reflecting unusual winter weather patterns, according to Katharine Abraham, commissioner of the department's Bureau of Labour Statistics.
"A longer term view suggests that underlying job groth in the (construction) industry has been quite strong," Abraham said in a prepared statement.
The department's household survey last month showed the number of job holders rising by 745,000 to 129.18 million, while the number of unemployed workers fell by 61,000 to 7.14 million.
The proportion of the American population that was employed last month rose to a record high 63.8 percent, the department said.
